A checkout service calls a payment provider. Code review approved it without comments: the
declaration, exactly as you'd treat any disposable. It passes every test. On the first real traffic peak, calls to the provider start failing with socket errors, and
on the server lists thousands of connections to the provider in the TIME_WAIT state. A colleague's quick fix, one
client for the whole app, stops the errors. A month later the provider moves to new IP addresses, and the service keeps calling the old ones until it's restarted.
, so the correct, careful thing is to create one per request and dispose it when the request is done.
That's the rule for almost everything else in .NET. Files, streams, database connections: if it's disposable, wrap it in
, and analyzers will remind you when you don't.

method. And the per-call version works perfectly in development and at low traffic, so nothing contradicts the rule until production does.
The rule assumes that disposing an object only cleans up after it. For
, disposing also throws away something expensive that was meant to be reused.
An HttpClient is a front for a connection pool

in .NET, and the handler owns a pool of open connections. Requests to the same server reuse a pooled connection, so the TCP and TLS handshakes happen once. When the client owns its handler, disposing the client disposes the handler and closes its connections. A new client per request means a new pool per request: a fresh connection, a fresh handshake, and a close, every time.
A closed connection keeps its port for a while

TCP doesn't release a port the moment a connection closes. The side that closes it keeps the port in the TIME-WAIT state for a period defined by the protocol. In a test on .NET 10, 1,000 sequential requests with
left 1,000 sockets in TIME_WAIT. The same 1,000 requests through one shared client, or through
, left none, and used a single connection. At a high request rate, that leftover state is what leads to
A client that lives forever never looks up DNS again
resolves a host name only when it opens a connection, and it ignores the DNS record's time to live. A pooled connection can stay open indefinitely, so a
client keeps talking to the IP it resolved at startup. That's the second half of the hook: the static client fixed the ports and broke failover. The fix is
, which closes connections after a set time so the next one resolves the name again.
. The factory keeps one handler per client name, and every

it hands out wraps the pooled handler. Disposing such a client doesn't dispose the handler, so it doesn't close connections. Handlers are recycled after their lifetime, two minutes by default, so new connections pick up DNS changes. The catch: the factory controls only the clients it hasn't handed out yet. Its clients are meant to be short-lived, and a client kept for hours keeps its old handler.
